claims.claim: the code's potential evapotranspiration, PET = 0.1651 · day length (12-h units) · saturated vapour density · KPEC mm/day, is Hamon's (1961)
claims.note: the 1961 article could not be read. Evidence against the attribution (not a confirmation either way): Hamon's 1960 MIT thesis of the same title gives the method as Ep = C·D²·Pt (Eq. 4, thesis pp. 36–37, PDF pp. 42–43; read on the page image): Ep in inches a day, D the possible hours of daily sunshine in units of 12 h, Pt the saturated water-vapour concentration (g/m³) at the mean temperature, C = 0.0055 — day length SQUARED, coefficient 0.0055 in = 0.1397 mm. The 1961 article's indexed abstract (Compendex, via OpenAlex; abstract only) also says 'day-time hours squared'. The code's form is linear in day length with 0.1651 mm (= 0.0065 in), as Lu et al. give it under the name 'Hamon (1963)'. The two agree near D ≈ 1.18 (≈14 h days) and part elsewhere: at D = 0.8 the linear form is ~48 % higher. Cite the form actually used (Lu et al. 2005) or switch to the D² form and cite Hamon 1961 once read.

notes: The code's 'Hamon' PET is not Hamon's 1961 formula as far as can be told without the article: Hamon's 1960 thesis (same title, the work the 1961 paper reports; stand-in, not the article) gives Ep = 0.0055·D²·Pt in/day (Eq. 4, pp. 36–37), with C = 0.0055 chosen so annual totals match Thornthwaite's at US stations (Table 1, p. 38); the 1961 article's indexed abstract says the same ('day-time hours squared'). The code uses Lu et al. 2005's Appendix A form, 0.1651·Ld·RHOSAT·KPEC, which Lu et al. attribute to Hamon (1963, IASH Publ. 63) and calibrate with KPEC 1.2 (Federer & Lash 1983's BROOK model; Sun et al. 2002); the code's KPEC is 1.0. 0.1651 mm is exactly 0.0065 in (my arithmetic, no source says so). Recommended: cite 'Hamon's PET as formulated by Lu et al. (2005)' (add Lu et al. 2005 to the references; it is free from the USDA Forest Service), and either drop Hamon 1961 or read it (ASCE; a library login) to say how the 1961 and 1963 forms differ. Lu et al. found Hamon among the three best PET methods for forested southeastern-US watersheds (abstract and p. 631), which supports the choice of method but is a warmer climate than Maine's.
